questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere outside of Europe and I had never been to Canada before. I didn't necessarily have any specific criteria, but I applied to different places in countries I wanted to visit/ live in.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy, however, the application process beforehand is quite extensive and difficult to navigate.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were multiple people to contact if you have questions and the respond time is fairly quick.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are different housing opportunities on campus - many different buildings as well as multiple kinds of residence options, such as single rooms, double rooms, shared apartments and so on.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: When you get residence on campus a meal plan is mandatory. There seemed to be different types of meal plans, but I never figured out how to change it, so it seemed like different meal plans, migth be assigned to different kinds of housing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
There is nothing in the residences and the building I lived in (Bates residence), was not a nice place. I was in several other buildings where the rooms and apartments were a lot better, however many of the apartments are designed in a suicide preventative way. 
You should expect spending money on items like a duvet, pillow, hangers, a fan (the aircondition in the building does not work, and the windows don't open more than 10cm), kitchen items - pans, pots, plates, knives etc. - and other basic necessities. I heard of an exchange student who got in touch with her roommates beforehand, and they arranged an agreement of who could bring different items, but still, if possible, I would search for a room in at least another building or off campus. 
Also, what I personally did not consider beforehand, is that people living on campus are first year students, which means that they are around 17-18 years old, and I think the age difference is a good thing to have in mind when applying to residence housing. 
An upside to living on campus is that you are close to all of your clases. 
You should also be aware that in the weekends and on some special occasions there are "guards" at the entrances of the building, so that you cannot bring guests, and if you do, they'll have to wear wristsbands and sign in (as do you) with student number and name.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Start to look for housing early!! Many students who didn't have an exact place to live from the beginning moved around the whole semester. But you might be able to find a place with other exchange students or even with locals. 
I would recommend arriving in Canada some time before, especially if you do not live on campus. There is a lot of scams in rentals in the nearby area, so being in the city and able to go see the places are a big plus. 
I recommend joining Facebook groups for Westdale especially - since it is the nearest and best area to stay close to campus.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
When you apply to the university, after having been submitted an exchange spot, you will be electing courses from the old course catalog. You need to be aware that you have to re-elect courses during the summer from the new catalog, any (in my case) many of the courses were not available for the semester I was there. 
When you do find course you would like, you will be asked to send a list of multiple courses to your academic advisor before a certain deadline, where you'll get some of them approved. You then need to register for the courses during a certain time period, where you can also choose a course schedule - I really recommend trying to plan your schedule so you can have some days off - especially Friday, it makes it easier to go on trips with others during a longer weekend.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There are multiple contact options available, but I would say it was still a pretty confusing process overall.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I ended up with most courses that i wanted, however - as I described - some courses you initially want might not be available for the fall term, and even if you get several courses approved by your academic advisor, some may be already full, reserved to specific students or not available for exchange students. And, as I described previously, it is possible to change your courses again after the term has begun.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take time to look at the courses and select a couple - and some back ups. Register for a couple courses that you think might be a little easier for you to follow, and be prepared to maybe not get every course you want and even if you do, it might not be what you thought, but still okay.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It is recommended that BA exchange students take level 3 courses. However, me and many of the others had courses on 1,2,3,4, level, which was not a problem.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I would say that the teaching style mostly differ from UCPH. 
You might be able to have courses approved for 7,5 ECTS points and if you can, I would recommend to do that so you can have 4 courses. Otherwise, you will have 5 courses in total during the semester, and there is a heavy workload - especially if you're in social sciences or humanities. I had around 4 written assignments per week, which put me under a lot of pressure - however, what's important to remember (and that i realized a little late) is that the academic level is different to the assignments you do on UCPH - it is a lot more direct and it is not expected that you do a lot of analyzing and research yourself - and if you need to, it is pretty easily done. You do, however, learn to just write and move on to the next thing, so that process in itself is a great quality. 
I would definetly also recommend that you consider taking some courses on different levels, and even taking some courses that you think may be a little easier for you to follow along in, because you will have a lot of work to do either way. 
You're professors are only doing lectures, the classes are held by Teaching Assistants (TA's), which themselves are either Master or Ph.D. students at the university. The classes (as I experienced), where mostly recapping what was said in lecture. However, they do take attendance at every class, and you need to be aware that attendance (as well as assignments, participation, quizzes, midterms and exams) holds different percentages of your final grade. 
You could, in a way, compare the system a bit more to high school in Denmark. 
 
There is around a weeks period in the beginning of the term, where you can change courses if you need to. However the deadline for this might be placed so you won't have had all of your courses, so it is a bit of a strange proces, but doable.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
There are no specific course I believe are recommendable - it all depends on your interests and if you want to try some different subjects. 
I had no subjects related to my original BA back home, which obviously made keeping up a bit harder, but I though it was interesting to try different subjects in other fields of study.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Trips, having to buy basic necessities for housing, souvenirs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Books, is not per month, but how much in total i spent on the books I needed to buy for my courses and they were fairly expensive.  
I lived on campus, where the expenses are payed all at once - including the payment for your mealcard, so that is the amount I've put.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are several events for international and exhange students. Some exchange students joined some of the sports teams. I recommend looking into the different events, and attending many of them - this is where you'll meet most people.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definetly recommend going on the MOOSE Exchange trip, that Mac Outdoor Club plans - this is where I met most people I hung out with for the rest of the exchange. It is a great way to bond with others when you first arrive in Canada. Also, the club offers multiple other trips and events during the semester, and I really recommend going on those. Me and a couple of my friends joined the Algonquin Canoe trip, which was great, and really beautiful - really a great opportunity to see some more of Canadian nature.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I recommend exploring the city a bit - I never really did, and I did not have a great experience of the city. 
Otherwise, I actually mostly recommend going to sportsgames in Toronto, or going on trips to Montreal, Ottawa, or other bigger cities in the province. We were a couple of students that planned a trip during the reading week, where we went to western Canada, and roadtripped around Vancouver, Banff, Jasper, Whistler and other absolutely beautiful places - I absolutely recommend doing this.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was easy. There are not big cultural differences, maybe other than saying thank you to the bus driver when leaving the bus, the school system and the general attitude towards talking to strangers - people are a lot more open to talk to others than they are in Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: There are not really any activities that bonds you with local students - some might be on some of the trips (if you go on those), so the only possibility you might have is in your classes. But mostly you'll hang out with other exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: It was interesting to experiences a more American culture, but there weren't any big differences, so I'm not sure.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be ready to talk to a lot of new people, be open and try to have the mentality of not saying no to anything, and remember that it is also okay to be overwhelmed (because you will be) and to stay home when you don't feel like going out or socializing.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Basically everyone is there to meet new people and have new experiences, talk to all the people you want and you'll eventually figure out who you naturally hang out with more, but don't exclude people from the beginning.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I've met and the memories I have made, both on trips and on fun nights on and off campus.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The school work load.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
Hamilton is not really a great place.. 
There are a lot of drug addicts and homeless people and it is overall a boring city, so the people you are with are important to your general experience. 

Also, if you're only there for one semester, do not apply for a study visa - you do not need one, and it takes a long time to do.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
